routes.description: Establish that Christian theism provides a rationally coherent account of nature, human reason, objective value, suffering, and human purpose, then connect that general theistic account to the biblical God through the historical claims concerning Jesus.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative scientific, philosophical, moral, existential, and historical considerations make belief in the biblical God rational while adequately addressing naturalistic alternatives, the evidential burden for miracles, and the challenge from undeserved suffering.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative case supports rational belief specifically in the biblical God, rather than merely an unspecified creator.

centralBridges.description: Show that cosmic order, intelligibility, and reliable rational minds are coherently explained by an ultimate rational creator.
Show that divine creation grounds objective morality, equal human worth, and an ultimate purpose not supplied by unguided processes alone.
Supply sufficient historical grounds for treating Jesus, the resurrection, and the New Testament witness as evidence identifying the creator with the biblical God.
Reconcile the biblical God's goodness and power with suffering through divine participation, compensation, justice, and enduring hope.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why stable natural laws do not logically exclude exceptional divine agency and why miracle claims remain open to historical assessment.
Distinguish evidence-responsive Christian commitment from unsupported belief and state the evidential role assigned to Gospel testimony.

routes.description: Establish that naturalistic explanations and secular accounts of reason, morality, meaning, and hope remove the need for a divine hypothesis, while suffering and weaknesses in the historical case count against belief in the biblical God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic and secular alternatives explain the relevant phenomena without God and if the proposed scientific, philosophical, moral, and historical grounds do not meet the burden required for rational belief in an omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good biblical deity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available considerations do not justify belief specifically in the biblical God under present standards of rational inquiry.

centralBridges.description: Show that cosmology, evolution, and natural processes can account for origins and apparent design without adding a divine explanatory entity.
Show that evolved rational capacities can track truth and support objective moral reasons without requiring a divine foundation.
Show that extensive undeserved human and nonhuman suffering is evidentially difficult to reconcile with the biblical God's asserted attributes.
Show that the evidence for resurrection, scriptural reliability, and Jesus's divine authority is insufficient for the extraordinary historical conclusions asserted.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for religious commitment through cultural transmission and require independent evidence capable of overcoming that contingency.
Show that finite purposes, practical efforts against suffering, and meaningful hope remain available without immortality or externally assigned purpose.

sections.title: Science, Origins, Design, and Rational Mind
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether cosmic intelligibility, apparent design, biological complexity, and reliable cognition favor an ultimate rational creator or are adequately explained by cosmology, evolution, and naturalistic accounts of mind.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Human Worth, and Purpose
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether objective moral reasons, equal human value, and ultimate purpose require creation in God's image or can arise through rational impartiality and self-directed secular purposes.

sections.title: Jesus, Resurrection, and Scriptural Reliability
sections.rationale: This issue supplies the necessary bridge from generic theism to the biblical God by testing the historical evidence for resurrection, the coherence of miracle claims, and the reliability and authority of New Testament testimony.

sections.title: Suffering, Hope, Compensation, and Justice
sections.rationale: This issue directly tests the compatibility of extensive undeserved suffering with the biblical God's goodness and power, alongside competing accounts of consolation, practical mitigation, afterlife compensation, and final justice.

sections.title: Faith, Cultural Contingency, and Explanatory Burden
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether invoking God improves explanation and whether Christian commitment is evidence-responsive despite concerns about unsupported faith, inherited religious affiliation, and the availability of an uncreated natural reality.

routes.description: Establish that the earliest recoverable traditions and independent attestations are better explained by a mortal Jewish teacher whose life and teachings were rapidly transformed through scriptural, epic, theological, and communal mythmaking.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by grounding Jesus in early independent tradition, explaining Pauline silence without positing an exclusively celestial Christ, defending external or interpersonal attestation, and showing that extensive Gospel invention remains compatible with an underlying historical person.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surviving early-source evidence to a first-century Jewish teacher whose subsequent mythologization does not erase his historical existence.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early tradition independent of Gospel literary invention that presents Jesus as a mortal Jewish teacher concerned with law and God's kingdom.
Explain Paul's sparse earthly biography through the purposes of his letters while identifying traditions or relationships that connect Paul to an earthly Jesus movement.
Defend Josephus's James reference and related early testimony as evidence independently anchoring Jesus and his followers in history.
Show how extensive literary and theological transformation can elevate and obscure a historical teacher without requiring that the earthly figure was invented.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for variations in kingdom, Torah, and mission traditions through changing communities and social identities.
Show that shared historical tradition explains the relevant overlaps and developments without unnecessary dependence on wholesale literary reification.

routes.description: Establish that the earliest evidence is more expected if Christianity began with a revelatory Christ and that later authors placed this figure into an earthly story through scriptural and literary reification unsupported by secure independent corroboration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by showing that Paul lacks expected traces of a recent earthly teacher, supplying a coherent revelatory and celestial origin model, explaining Gospel biography as later literary construction, and defeating purported independent attestations or demonstrations that the evidence discriminates in favor of historicity.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidentiary pattern of early revelation and later historicization to the proposition that Christianity began without a recent earthly founder.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's repeated reliance on revelation and scripture, together with missing expected earthly references, differentially supports a revelatory-Christ origin.
Provide a historically coherent account in which an incarnate Christ is killed by supernatural powers and known to apostles through revelation.
Explain earthly Gospel narratives as literary transformations of Pauline, scriptural, communal, or revelatory materials rather than memories of a teacher.
Show that Josephus, kinship language, eyewitness claims, and later Christian texts do not securely provide independent attestation of a historical Jesus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require contextual evidence that distinguishes historical-memory explanations from revelatory or literary-reification alternatives.
Constrain reconstruction according to the chronology, dependence, ambiguity, and scarcity of the surviving sources.

sections.title: Paul, revelation, and traces of an earthly life
sections.rationale: Paul is the earliest major evidence in dispute, and the competing explanations of his biographical omissions, revealed knowledge, teachings, and personal contacts directly distinguish the two origin models.

sections.title: Q, Jewish teaching, and kingdom traditions
sections.rationale: The status and independence of traditions about Torah reform, mission, apocalypse, and God's kingdom determine whether an early mortal teacher is recoverable before later Gospel composition.

sections.title: Gospel mythmaking and literary reification
sections.rationale: Both routes must explain how earthly narratives arose, including whether epic and scriptural transformation presupposes a historical subject or can manufacture one from prior revelatory and communal material.

sections.title: Josephus, James, and independent attestation
sections.rationale: The identification of James, the meaning and transmission of the kinship wording, and the legal context determine whether the debate has significant external evidence for Jesus.

sections.title: Later testimony, alternative Christians, and evidential method
sections.rationale: Johannine, Papian, Ignatian, Petrine, and Acts traditions test competing claims about eyewitness memory and early dissent, while comparative standards govern what these sparse sources can establish.

routes.description: Establish that possible conscious experiences and the causal relations among them are factual features of reality capable of supporting objective distinctions between better and worse ways for conscious beings to live.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if facts about consciousness identify genuine differences in well-being, permit discoverable navigation among possible states, and remain normatively significant despite contingent preferences and the first-person character of experience.

motionBridge.description: Show that facts about conscious well-being can ground objective evaluative guidance rather than merely implement independently chosen ends.

centralBridges.description: Establish a factual landscape of possible conscious states containing materially better and worse conditions and causal routes between them.
Explain why inherited or modifiable preferences do not exhaust the standards by which possible changes in experience are evaluated.
Connect discoverable facts about navigating conscious experience to objectively right and wrong practical directions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for the reality of values instantiated in consciousness despite their essentially first-person mode of appearance.
Allow for attainable goods that agents may fail to recognize because of empirical cognitive, emotional, or cultural limitations.

routes.description: Establish that ethical language expresses attitudes or directives while science supplies objective information only about how conscious systems can realize ends selected through subjective preferences.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if preferences, including higher-order preferences, can explain the selection of ends and if empirical facts can explain effective pursuit of those ends without entailing objective moral truth, obligation, or prescription.

motionBridge.description: Show that emotive expression plus instrumental facts can account for ethical discourse and practical coordination without objective morality.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish expressing an attitude through moral language from reporting a truth-apt fact about possessing that attitude.
Separate subjective selection of experiential ends from objective scientific knowledge about the means of attaining them.
Explain preference change, cooperation, flourishing, and informed action without introducing objective moral properties or prescriptions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for voluntary alteration of preferences through higher-order desires rather than an independent moral standard.
Locate value in the commitments of conscious systems while preserving objective facts about effective action.

sections.title: The semantic status of ethical language
sections.rationale: The dispute requires an account of whether moral utterances state objective propositions, report subjective states, or instead express attitudes and directives.

sections.title: Experiential landscapes and the ends-means distinction
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether factual knowledge of possible conscious states and causal routes establishes evaluative destinations or only serves antecedently selected ends.

sections.title: Preference revision and higher-order desire
sections.rationale: The treatment of contingent and scientifically alterable preferences determines whether preference change requires a further evaluative standard or remains preference-relative.

sections.title: Subjective experience and the reality of value
sections.rationale: The debate turns partly on whether value's first-person manifestation undermines objectivity or identifies a real feature of conscious systems that facts can track.

sections.title: Practical flourishing and objective moral direction
sections.rationale: This issue asks whether a complete practical account of cooperation, discovery, flourishing, misery avoidance, and experiential navigation entails objective moral direction.

routes.description: Establish that conscious experience resists reductive materialist explanation, that nonphysical mind remains coherent, and that a prior divine consciousness supplies the ultimate ground of finite conscious minds.
routes.successCriteria: Connect the inadequacy of reductive and merely structural accounts to a positive, non-gaps explanation in which divine consciousness makes the existence and character of human consciousness intelligible while remaining compatible with scientific mechanisms.

motionBridge.description: Show that consciousness calls for an ultimate personal ground and that divine consciousness supplies that ground beyond a merely non-theistic account.

centralBridges.description: Establish that neural correlations and quantitative descriptions do not entail that physical brains exhaustively produce or explain qualitative experience.
Establish that nonphysical mind and mind-body interaction are coherent enough to remain live alternatives to reductive or emergent physicalism.
Show that treating consciousness as fundamental within matter leaves unresolved its ultimate origin or the formation of unified complex subjects.
Provide a positive account connecting finite human consciousness to a prior personal divine consciousness without displacing scientific accounts of mechanism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend first-person consciousness as unavoidable evidence by explaining why attempts to dismiss it as illusion depend on the phenomenon they deny.
Explain how a personal divine ground bears on the intelligibility of conscious persons and their capacity for relationship and meaning.

routes.description: Establish that materialism omits qualitative consciousness, that panpsychism integrates experience with the physical world parsimoniously, and that neither consciousness nor remaining theoretical questions warrant an inference to God.
routes.successCriteria: Supply a coherent non-theistic account of consciousness as matter's intrinsic nature, address the transition from simple to complex experience sufficiently for the comparative burden, and show that adding divine consciousness does not provide a necessary or more informative explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that a non-theistic panpsychist framework can explain consciousness without the evidential or explanatory addition of God.

centralBridges.description: Establish that physical science describes quantitative structure and behavior while leaving the qualitative character of experience unexplained.
Show that consciousness can coherently occupy the intrinsic nature of matter left unspecified by physics while preserving the physical structure science describes.
Establish that panpsychism can unify physical structure and qualitative experience with fewer additional commitments than dualist or theistic alternatives.
Show that making consciousness fundamental or identifying unresolved combination questions does not specifically support God as an explanatory conclusion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide an intelligible research or principle-based path by which simple experiential constituents could form unified and increasingly complex consciousness.
Clarify why consciousness requires philosophical comparison alongside empirical correlation and cannot be adjudicated by direct external observation alone.

sections.title: Materialism, neuroscience, and qualitative experience
sections.rationale: The shared starting issue is whether neural correlation and quantitative physical description can account for first-person qualities, setting the explanatory burden for every proposed alternative.

sections.title: Competing mind ontologies and parsimony
sections.rationale: The debate requires comparison among physicalist emergence, substance dualism, and panpsychism, including whether each view makes mind-body relations intelligible with proportionate commitments.

sections.title: Panpsychism as a positive account of matter and consciousness
sections.rationale: The non-theistic route depends on more than rejecting materialism: it must explain how consciousness can constitute matter's intrinsic nature, while the pro route tests whether that account reaches consciousness's ultimate source.

sections.title: Combination, evolution, and complex conscious subjects
sections.rationale: A fundamental-consciousness view must connect simple experience to unified complex minds, and this issue determines whether panpsychism supplies a continuous natural account or retains a major explanatory transition.

sections.title: Divine grounding and the inference to God
sections.rationale: This is the motion-level clash over whether divine consciousness positively grounds finite minds or instead adds an unnecessary layer that neither resolves mind ontology nor follows from gaps in panpsychism.

routes.description: Establish the motion through a cumulative case in which the universe's beginning requires a transcendent personal cause, objective moral values require a divine foundation, and the historical facts concerning Jesus are best explained by divine resurrection, while answering principal naturalistic objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cosmological, moral, and resurrection inferences jointly warrant a transcendent personal and moral foundation of reality, and if objections from naturalistic explanation, suffering, source reliability, and methodological limits do not defeat those inferences.

motionBridge.description: The supported cosmological, moral, and historical conclusions must jointly warrant that God exists as the transcendent personal cause and moral foundation of reality.

centralBridges.description: The universe must have begun to exist, and its beginning must require a transcendent, immaterial, personal cause rather than emergence from non-being.
Objective moral values and duties must be real and must require a transcendent divine foundation that evolutionary or social accounts do not supply.
The historical facts concerning Jesus must be established and divine resurrection must explain them better than the proposed natural alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The existence of suffering must remain compatible with God through the possibility of morally sufficient reasons for permitting it.
Philosophical reasoning must legitimately draw metaphysical consequences from scientifically informed premises without depending on an appeal to unexplained gaps.

routes.description: Defeat the motion by showing that no observed feature of reality requires God, that naturalistic accounts or open scientific inquiry remain available for cosmic origins, morality, and reported miracles, and that suffering conflicts with the proposed loving deity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative inferences fail to establish their divine conclusions because their premises or explanatory bridges remain unsupported, natural alternatives remain viable, and the evidential challenge from suffering is not adequately reconciled with an all-loving God.

motionBridge.description: The motion fails if the universe, morality, and historical reports do not require a transcendent personal and moral foundation and the total evidence supplies no adequate basis for God.

centralBridges.description: Cosmic beginning, physical constants, and apparent order must admit naturalistic possibilities without requiring pre-universe causality, purpose, or a divine creator.
Moral conduct and distinctions must be explicable through biological and social development without requiring a divine source or judge.
The resurrection inference must lack sufficiently reliable historical evidence, with ordinary explanations remaining more credible than suspension of natural law.
Apparently gratuitous innocent suffering must count against the existence of the all-loving God specified by the affirmative position.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Claims about reality must be constrained by observation and testable theorizing rather than by metaphysical extrapolation or untestable divine intentions.
A divine entity must not be introduced when simpler explanations remain available in principle or scientific inquiry has not exhausted natural accounts.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Causality, and a Personal First Cause
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal clash over whether the universe began, whether causality applies to that beginning, whether net-zero or successive-universe accounts alter the origin problem, and whether any required cause is personal and transcendent.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Its Foundation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether objective moral values and duties exist, whether evolutionary and social accounts explain only moral behavior or also binding validity, and whether a transcendent divine foundation is required by the motion.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Miracle Inference
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the empty tomb, reported appearances, and origin of Christian belief are historically established, whether the sources are reliable, and whether divine resurrection is warranted over natural explanations.

sections.title: Suffering and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This issue matters because apparently gratuitous innocent suffering is offered as evidence against an all-loving God, while the opposing route requires showing that God could have morally sufficient reasons for permitting it.

sections.title: Scientific Explanation, Philosophy, and Divine Necessity
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether scientific evidence may support premises with theological consequences, whether metaphysical reasoning legitimately extends beyond empirical inquiry, and whether natural explanation makes God unnecessary without merely appealing to future discovery.

routes.description: Establish that Bignon's experience, providentially interpreted coincidences, and supporting intellectual and historical considerations can jointly provide rational support for specifically Christian belief without compelling every observer.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the experiential pattern is rationally relevant under a comparative explanation, rival experiences do not neutralize it, and independent considerations can support its Christian interpretation at the modest standard of personal rational justification.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conversion experience and supporting considerations jointly make Christian belief rationally supportable despite naturalist and rival-religion alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Explain why the personally salient convergence of experiences and coincidences is more expected under providence than under an unaided naturalistic account.
Connect experience with intellectual considerations so the case supplies rational justification without requiring coercive or universally compelling proof.
Provide a principled way to distinguish the Christian interpretation from incompatible religious experiences through comparative intellectual and historical considerations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for why providential guidance in one conversion need not imply equivalent guidance or conversion opportunities for every person.
Clarify how surviving early Christian materials can aid access to historical claims without treating their abundance alone as proof of those claims.

routes.description: Establish that reverse conversions, culturally variable experiences, ordinary coincidence, and competing intellectual considerations remove any distinctive evidential advantage claimed for Bignon's Christian interpretation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic explanations adequately predict conversion patterns, rival experiences resist a uniquely Christian reading, and the proposed intellectual or historical adjudicators do not restore a clear evidential advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that rival experiences and naturalistic explanations undercut the claimed evidential force of Bignon's experience for specifically Christian belief.

centralBridges.description: Explain how large populations, ordinary coincidence, and culturally familiar narratives can generate apparently coordinated conversion stories without providential causation.
Show how culturally diverse and directionally opposed religious experiences weaken an inference from personal experience to Christianity in particular.
Establish that philosophical and historical considerations remain contested and do not plainly break the symmetry between Christian, rival-religious, and naturalist interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether selective providential intervention fits the persistence of reasonable nonbelief and the uneven distribution of conversion experiences.
Distinguish evidential quality from documentary quantity by considering how institutional dominance and preservation affect the surviving record.

sections.title: Providential pattern or natural coincidence
sections.rationale: This section addresses the primary explanatory clash over whether the conversion story's coordinated and personally salient events favor divine providence or are expected among many lives shaped by ordinary coincidence and familiar narratives.

sections.title: Personal justification and the cumulative case
sections.rationale: This section fixes the relevant epistemic burden and examines how experience, philosophical argument, and background considerations may combine to support belief without forcing rational convergence or excluding reasonable disagreement.

sections.title: Rival religious experiences and Christian specificity
sections.rationale: This section tests whether culturally diverse experiences, reverse conversions, and disputed exceptions neutralize specifically Christian support, or whether different experiences can be compared without dismissing all experiential evidence.

sections.title: Historical and intellectual adjudication
sections.rationale: This section considers whether historical sources and broader intellectual arguments can adjudicate between Christianity and rival interpretations when experiential claims appear balanced, including the significance and limits of the surviving documentary record.

sections.title: Selective providence and persistent nonbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether a providential account of one person's conversion can accommodate uneven divine guidance, persistent reasonable nonbelief, and competing considerations concerning hiddenness without undermining the proposed explanation.

routes.description: Establish that the canonical Gospels preserve historically trustworthy accounts by connecting informed provenance, Palestinian contextual knowledge, coherent transmission, and continuity in their presentation of Jesus to a cumulative inference of reliability.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its provenance and internal features provide a warranted connection to early informed tradition, withstand the principal transmission, discrepancy, and developmental objections, and jointly support trust in the accounts covered by the motion.

motionBridge.description: Show that the relevant Gospel accounts collectively warrant historical trust concerning Jesus' life, teaching, death, and resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Connect authorship, research, source access, chronology, and Palestinian knowledge to informed and sufficiently early provenance.
Explain why the pattern of contextual detail, names, and literary features favors preserved tradition over substantial alteration.
Account for alleged discrepancies and differences in coverage without requiring historical incompatibility or fabrication.
Establish meaningful continuity between earlier Gospel presentations of Jesus and John's distinctive claims and themes.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify how assumptions about prediction, miracles, or naturalism bear on dating and evaluation of the traditions.
Integrate independent contextual, literary, chronological, and thematic features into the motion-level inference.

routes.description: Establish that the canonical Gospels cannot be treated as reliable throughout by connecting delayed and uncertain provenance, mutable oral transmission, substantive narrative tensions, and theological development to the need for claim-by-claim historical discrimination.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed transmission history and specific textual comparisons show that accurate background details can coexist with altered, incompatible, or developed central claims, thereby defeating an inference to reliability across the accounts.

motionBridge.description: Show that the canonical accounts contain enough historically consequential alteration or conflict to preclude treating them as reliable throughout.

centralBridges.description: Establish the temporal, linguistic, authorial, and source-access gaps between Jesus and the written accounts.
Explain how oral and literary transmission could preserve incidental setting details while changing central stories and teachings.
Use comparison of parallel accounts to determine whether material differences resist a single factual reconstruction.
Trace whether later distinctive claims about Jesus reflect theological development absent from multiple earlier sources.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require historical conclusions and proposed harmonizations to remain revisable in light of textual and archaeological evidence.
Maintain the distinction between accurate contextual information and the truth of the narratives' central reported events.

sections.title: Authorship, Dating, and Access to Early Sources
sections.rationale: The temporal distance, identities, research practices, and source access of the Gospel writers determine how directly the written accounts can be connected to informed early testimony.

sections.title: Palestinian Knowledge and Its Evidential Reach
sections.rationale: Geography, customs, measures, language, and personal-name patterns form a major shared clash over whether accurate setting information supports the truth and transmission of central claims.

sections.title: Oral Transmission, Parallel Accounts, and Discrepancies
sections.rationale: Competing models of preservation and change, tested through parallel narratives and proposed reconciliations, directly bear on whether the accounts can be relied upon across disputed factual reports.

sections.title: Continuity and Development in the Portrait of Jesus
sections.rationale: Differences between the Synoptic traditions and John concerning Jesus' teaching and divine identity bear on whether consequential material reflects authentic continuity or later theological development.

sections.title: Historical Method and the Cumulative Reliability Inference
sections.rationale: The treatment of prediction, miracles, prior commitments, textual integrity, and converging features governs how the underlying evidence may be combined into or withheld from a motion-level conclusion.

routes.description: Establish ordinary stance-independent moral objectivity, support an ontology of normative facts through deliberative indispensability, and show that rival-package challenges neither create a genuine deliberative gap nor impose a distinctive comparative liability on realism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if stance-independent normative facts remain a justified account of ordinary moral objectivity, an agent's first-person conclusion about what ought to be done can settle deliberation, and iterative rival-package objections do not supply a burden-defeating reason to reject realism.

motionBridge.description: Connect stance-independent normative truth to action by requiring that a first-person conclusion about what ought to be done normally completes deliberation without an additional allegiance decision.

centralBridges.description: Explain why ordinary moral claims presuppose independence from preferences and conventions and why this supports realist normative facts.
Supply an affirmative basis for normative facts by showing their indispensable role in deliberation and practical reasoning.
Answer the privilege regress by explaining why iteration does not establish a genuine further normative question or a distinctive objection to realism.
Compare theories by their treatment of central deliberative practice while assigning proportionate significance to rare reflective anomalies.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify the additional commitments required for a non-cognitivist alternative to preserve ordinary claims of moral objectivity.
Explain when justified confidence can terminate iterative philosophical challenges without requiring persuasion of every skeptical or confused agent.

routes.description: Distinguish mind-independent moral properties from action-settling objectivity, demonstrate that metaphysical privilege cannot determine allegiance among rival normative packages, and develop an attitude-centered alternative that closes the remaining gap between normative representation and decision.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if rival stance-independent packages leave an intelligible further question about what to do, neither nonnormative nor normative privilege resolves that question without regress, and an alternative account can connect normative judgment to action more directly than realist facts alone.

motionBridge.description: Show that the existence and recognition of stance-independent normative facts can leave unresolved which rival normative package an agent should follow in acting.

centralBridges.description: Establish that nonnormative metaphysical privilege is practically inert while normative privilege recreates the rival-package question at a higher level.
Use informed reflective disputes to show that knowledge of normative or logical facts need not non-causally settle an agent's deliberation.
Explain how deciding, prescribing, or adopting an action-directed attitude can exclude incompatible actions without requiring allegiance among rival truth-apt properties.
Defend the evidential importance of foundational anomalies even when they are rare, abstract, or do not amount to a classical contradiction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show how an attitude-centered alternative might avoid dependence on the full semantic machinery associated with standard expressivism.
Separate denial of true contradictions from questions about legitimate consequence relations and the comparative severity of theoretical costs.

sections.title: Ordinary objectivity and the realist foundation
sections.rationale: This issue fixes what stance independence amounts to, whether ordinary moral discourse supports robust realist facts, and whether deliberative indispensability supplies an affirmative basis for their ontology.

sections.title: Rival normative packages and metaphysical privilege
sections.rationale: This is the governing clash over whether metaphysical privilege can identify the action-guiding normative package or instead becomes practically inert or recursively contested.

sections.title: Non-cognitivism as a comparative alternative
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether an attitude-centered account can connect normative judgment with decision while still accommodating the ordinary objectivity that motivates realism.

sections.title: First-person deliberation and reflective counterexamples
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether concluding that one ought to act normally settles deliberation and whether rare, informed disputes reveal a genuine residual choice among normative standards.

sections.title: Theoretical costs, anomalies, and legitimate stopping points
sections.rationale: This issue governs how much weight to assign explanatory anomalies, contradictions, exceptional cases, and iterative skeptical challenges when comparing accounts of normative objectivity.

routes.description: Establish reasonable theism through a cumulative inference that a personal transcendent source better explains cosmic origins and fine-tuning, consciousness and rationality, objective morality and dignity, and the intelligibility of evil than naturalism does.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its principal phenomena remain evidentially significant, the theistic account explains them with greater unity and adequacy than the relevant naturalistic alternatives, and objections concerning suffering and religious history do not defeat the resulting reasonableness claim.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative comparative case to reasonable belief in general theism without requiring that any single argument prove Christianity or establish certainty.

centralBridges.description: Show that cosmic beginning conditions and life-permitting fine-tuning are better explained by a transcendent intelligent cause than by physical self-sufficiency, chance, or brute fact.
Show that consciousness and truth-directed rational faculties fit a reality grounded in supreme mind better than strict materialist naturalism.
Show that objective value, duty, and intrinsic human dignity require a foundation supplied by God's non-arbitrary good character and the divine image.

Explain why suffering and religious corruption do not overturn the cumulative case, including how objective evil remains intelligible and how abuses may be distinguished from Christianity's proper ethical standard.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the relevance of comparing theism with representative naturalistic commitments while acknowledging that cosmological evidence initially supports general rather than specifically biblical theism.
Support the moral case by clarifying disputed Christian teachings and identifying internal resources for moral correction and reform.

routes.description: Deny that the cumulative case makes belief in God reasonable by showing that its empirical and philosophical inferences are underdetermined, that naturalistic alternatives remain available, and that suffering and the historical record of religious explanation count against the proposed God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative phenomena do not discriminate adequately in favor of a personal benevolent creator, unresolved questions cannot properly be converted into theistic evidence, and the counterevidence from natural history and religious performance substantially weakens the cumulative inference.

motionBridge.description: Show that gaps in present naturalistic explanation and the bare compatibility of phenomena with theism do not satisfy the burden for reasonable belief in God.

centralBridges.description: Challenge both an absolute cosmic beginning and the probabilistic design inference by presenting the universe's scale, repeated opportunities, and divine omnipotence as complications for fine-tuning evidence.
Show that naturalism and atheism need not entail a single strict materialist package, so uncertainty about consciousness, freedom, or abstract objects is not affirmative evidence for God.
Argue that cosmic vastness, evolutionary waste, extinction, and pervasive suffering are less expected under an omnipotent benevolent creator than under naturalism.
Argue that the replacement of religious explanations and the revision of inherited moral teachings undermine claims of reliable revelation and superior theistic explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Offer evolutionary accounts of moral sentiments and invoke the Euthyphro challenge to contest the claim that objective morality uniquely requires God.
Explain religious moral change as externally pressured adaptation or selective survival rather than evidence that fixed religious authority reliably generates reform.

sections.title: Cumulative Inference and the Scope of the Worldview Comparison
sections.rationale: Frames what must be shown for belief to be reasonable, whether an inference to the best explanation may aggregate several clues, and which forms of theism and naturalism are legitimately compared.

sections.title: Cosmic Origins, Scale, and Fine-Tuning
sections.rationale: Tests whether beginning conditions and life-permitting parameters favor a transcendent designer or remain underdetermined given cosmic scale, chance opportunities, uncertainty about an absolute beginning, and divine omnipotence.

sections.title: Consciousness, Rational Faculties, and Naturalistic Commitments
sections.rationale: Examines whether consciousness and truth-directed reasoning require a supreme mind, whether evolution undermines cognitive reliability, and whether naturalism must accept the strict materialism targeted by those arguments.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and Human Dignity
sections.rationale: Addresses whether objective value, obligation, and intrinsic human worth need a divine foundation, alongside the Euthyphro dilemma and evolutionary or goal-relative naturalistic accounts of morality.

sections.title: Evil, Suffering, and the Shape of Natural History
sections.rationale: Weighs evolutionary suffering, extinction, cosmic vastness, and apparent waste against the claim that evil presupposes objective norms and can ultimately be defeated within a theistic framework.

sections.title: Religious Explanation, Revelation, and Moral Reform
sections.rationale: Evaluates Christianity's asserted moral influence and internal corrective resources against alleged explanatory displacement, disputed teachings, institutional resistance to reform, and revision of positions concerning women and sexuality.

routes.description: Establish Christian theism as more plausible than skeptical agnosticism through a cumulative case from cosmic fine-tuning and origin, objective morality, the resurrection and Christian revelation, and experiences of numinous beauty, while accounting for evolutionary suffering and the absence of coercive proof.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the converging considerations are reasonably explained by a loving, orderly creator and specifically support Christian commitment, with the evidential force of the whole exceeding the skeptical alternatives and the counterevidence from suffering and uncertainty.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence makes Christian theism more plausible than skeptical agnosticism.

centralBridges.description: Connect cosmic existence and life-permitting physical constants to an intelligent, orderly creator rather than an unexplained or multiverse alternative.
Connect historical resurrection claims and revelation to Christianity rather than merely generic creator theism.
Show that morality and beauty reinforce the scientific and historical considerations as a cumulative case despite uncertainty.
Explain why evolutionary and physical suffering remain compatible with a loving God who creates through stable natural laws.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend rational commitment on substantial but noncoercive evidence rather than requiring mathematical proof.
Explain how divine purposes may operate through physical, evolutionary, and neural mechanisms without competing with them.

routes.description: Establish skeptical agnosticism as the more warranted position by showing that the concept of God and the proposed evidence underdetermine Christian theism, that fine-tuning admits reversal or alternatives, that resurrection and public-revelation claims lack sufficient historical support, and that extensive suffering weighs against a loving creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the named considerations remain mysteries or support multiple explanations rather than preferentially supporting Christianity, especially when the improbability of apparently avoidable suffering under loving-creator theism is included in the comparative assessment.

motionBridge.description: Show that the total evidence does not warrant preferring Christian theism to skeptical agnosticism.

centralBridges.description: Show that disputed or incomprehensible divine attributes prevent the evidence from identifying the Christian God with adequate confidence.
Show that narrow physical constraints may be unexpected under omnipotent creation and do not uniquely favor a creator.
Show that extensive apparently avoidable evolutionary suffering is more expected under naturalism than under a loving creator.
Show that source-critical uncertainty and limits on private revelation weaken the move from generic possibility to Christianity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve naturalistic, evolutionary, legendary-development, and other rival explanations for the cited phenomena.
Distinguish acknowledging profound mysteries and existential stakes from claiming that they justify confident belief.

sections.title: Fine-tuning, cosmic explanation, and divine power
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal scientific case for an intelligent creator and the central skeptical challenge that physical fine-tuning may constrain or count against an omnipotent God, including multiverse and ultimate-explanation alternatives.

sections.title: Evolutionary suffering and orderly creation
sections.rationale: The comparative expectations of naturalism and loving-creator theism turn substantially on animal suffering, predation, extinction, and physical evil, together with the claim that stable natural laws and divine purposes explain their presence.

sections.title: Resurrection, Christian revelation, and historical warrant
sections.rationale: The resurrection and revelation are required to move the case from generic theism to Christianity, while Gospel source criticism, legendary development, martyrdom claims, Pauline testimony, and the public limits of private experience bear on that move.

sections.title: Morality, beauty, and transcendent experience
sections.rationale: Objective moral experience and numinous beauty provide distinct proposed signs of transcendence, while biblical moral concerns, aesthetic diversity, emotional and evolutionary accounts, and skeptical concessions define their comparative evidential reach.

sections.title: Cumulative evidence, uncertainty, and warranted commitment
sections.rationale: The debate ultimately compares a cumulative rationale for noncoercive Christian commitment with agnostic restraint toward several acknowledged mysteries, making standards of proof, conceptual clarity, combined evidential force, and existential significance burden-relevant.
